processing: Leaves of the garden raspberry, Rubus idaeus, are dried and cut with no further processing.
harvest_season: Not tied to a prized picking; sold dried year round.
appearance_dry: Crumbly cut leaf, dull green with paler, slightly downy undersides.
appearance_liquor: Little is recorded; as with other dried leaf herbs, expect a clear yellow to light amber.
taste_profile: Reliable tasting notes are scarce in the sources; expect a mild herbal cup with some astringency, as is typical of dried leaf herbs, and no raspberry flavour should be assumed.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for dried leaf herbs, not an established recipe. Shorten the steep if it turns drying.

vintage_note: Sold with no vintage, loose or in bags, under a best-before date. As with other dried leaf, the fresher pack is better. Packs can be marketed heavily at pregnant women, and that claim is not well supported.
description:
Raspberry leaf tea is made from the leaf of the garden raspberry, Rubus idaeus. It is a leaf herb, so do not assume it will taste of the fruit.

The leaf is simply dried and cut. Tasting notes are scarce in the sources, so treat it as a plain herbal cup and steep to taste.

Its fame comes from pregnancy lore: it has long been recommended as an aid to childbirth. Research has found little to no support, and a 2009 review called the recommendations questionable and raised concern over the missing safety evidence. Anyone pregnant should ask a midwife or doctor rather than go by the packet.
history:
Raspberry leaf belongs to folk medicine, and it is listed as a herbal drug under the name Rubi idaei folium. Russian herbal references list raspberry tea as sweat-inducing, astringent and anti-inflammatory, and English-speaking lore connects the leaf with childbirth.

The evidence for the childbirth use is largely anecdotal, and how far back the custom goes is not reliably dated. A 2009 review pointed out the absence of good evidence on safety or efficacy.
